Europe’s ammunition drive hits cotton supply bottleneck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:20:32 UTC
21:20:32 KST

155 mm N795 artillery projectiles are stored during manufacturing process. (AP photo)
Europe’s efforts to expand ammunition production are running into a shortage of cotton linters, a little-known raw material needed to manufacture propellants for artillery shells and other munitions.
Cotton linters are the short fibers left on cotton seeds after the longer fibers used by the textile industry have been removed. Once purified, their high cellulose content makes them suitable for producing nitrocellulose, the principal ingredient in smokeless propellants.
The propellant burns rapidly inside a weapon, generating the gas needed to launch a projectile. It is separate from the explosive charge carried by an artillery shell.
Demand has risen sharply since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, rapidly depleting European ammunition stocks. Production of NATO-standard 155 mm shells has increased, but shortages of nitrocellulose and other inputs have limited how quickly manufacturers can expand output.
The Wall Street Journal reported that limited linter supplies remained one of the main obstacles to NATO’s efforts to replenish its ammunition reserves. European nitrocellulose capacity would need to more than double to about 20,000 tons a year to meet projected demand, according to estimates cited by the newspaper.
Europe’s reliance on China has added to concerns over security of supply. Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger said in 2024 that European producers obtained more than 70 percent of their cotton linters from China.
The issue also has direct relevance for Türkiye, which produces both cotton and military-grade nitrocellulose.
The state-owned Mechanical and Chemical Industry Corporation’s (MKE) Powder Factory in the central province of Kırıkkale already manufactures several types of nitrocellulose and propellant powder for small- and large-caliber ammunition.
MKE is also building the Hüseyin Kâhya Energetic Materials Factory in Kırıkkale as part of its investment program covering 2023-2027. The facility is scheduled to begin production in 2026 and will manufacture nitrocellulose, gunpowder, rocket fuel, concentrated nitric acid and solid TNT.
The Defense Ministry has said the investment will approximately triple Türkiye’s existing production capacity for gunpowder, rocket fuel and explosives while reducing dependence on imported chemicals.
Türkiye’s cotton cultivation and processing industry could provide access to linter feedstock as European manufacturers seek alternatives to China. However, raw cotton or yarn production does not by itself amount to an ammunition supply capability.
Linters must be separated, purified and converted into military-grade nitrocellulose at specialized chemical plants that operate under strict safety and quality requirements. No plans to export output from MKE’s new facility have been announced.

Japan to Develop Hypersonic Missile for Submarines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:19:36 UTC
21:19:36 KST

The Japan Ministry of Defense has requested funding in the fiscal 2027 budget to develop a hypersonic missile for submarines.
Kyodo News reported this.
The development of such a missile would be a new program intended to strengthen the strike capabilities of Japan’s submarine fleet.
The official budget request document has not yet been published. However, Japan is already developing a vertical launch system for cruise and ballistic missiles that is planned for use on submarines.
The new program comes as Japan Ministry of Defense is seeking a record budget to finance the Self-Defense Forces. The request for ¥8.9 trillion, or about $60.1 billion, is intended to support the development of new methods of warfare.
Despite the budget request, development of hypersonic weapons, including hypersonic cruise missiles, has been underway since 2019. In December 2025, Japan Ministry of Defense announced that it was beginning mass production of new hypersonic guided missiles to strengthen the country’s long-range defense capabilities.
Although the full development cycle is not expected to be completed until fiscal 2031, Japan’s military command has decided not to wait until then. Following successful interim research results from work that began in 2023, Japan decided to begin mass production.
Read also: “Japan’s Missile Era: Short- and Medium-Range Ballistic Missiles.”
In June 2026, Militarnyi reported that development of the vertical launch system would continue from 2026 to 2029, with total research costs estimated at about ¥3.9 billion ($24.8 million).
Engineers are developing a vertical launch system capable of launching various types of missiles, including HVGP ballistic missiles, specifically the naval variant, as well as cruise and hypersonic missiles.
According to the officially released rendering, the system will have seven to eight cells in each launch module for storing missiles. A submarine will be able to carry two to three such systems, with a total of 14 to 24 cells.
Meanwhile, in October 2025, Japan Ministry of Defense awarded a contract for the mass production of new cruise missiles for surface warships and submarines.
The missiles are 12SSM-ER missiles, which will become the Japan Self-Defense Forces’ standardized primary long-range weapon for the Navy, Air Force and Ground Self-Defense Force.

African state joins Trump deportation drive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:17:26 UTC
21:17:26 KST

African state joins Trump deportation drive
Liberia has agreed to accept up to 1,200 third-country migrants deported from the US under a controversial agreement pushed by the Trump administration as part of its sweeping immigration crackdown.
The transfers will take place over one year, with the first group of 20 due to arrive in the West African country on Thursday, Liberia’s Ministry of Information said in a statement on Tuesday.
The arrangement, concluded through an exchange of diplomatic notes in September 2025, covers medically cleared nationals of “African and Western Hemisphere countries.” Those transferred may apply for asylum in Liberia or leave the country voluntarily, the ministry stated.
It said the deportees “are not criminals” and will be treated as guests rather than prisoners. The government said it would provide protection and support during their stay.
Monrovia insisted that the arrangement “is not a transaction with a quid pro quo” and that Liberia “has not demanded or received any compensation or promise of reward.” However, it said the country “will receive support to help manage the program and strengthen its migration system more broadly,” without disclosing the value or terms of the assistance.
The deal is among the largest reached under US President Donald Trump’s expanding third-country deportation policy. The mechanism allows Washington to remove migrants to states where they hold no citizenship or established ties, including when their home governments refuse to receive them.
A coalition of rights lawyers and advocates, including the Global Strategic Litigation Council, has accused Washington of using third-country transfers to bypass protection orders and expose migrants to persecution or torture. Thousands have reportedly been transferred to nearly two dozen states, including around ten in Africa.
Ghana, Eswatini, Rwanda, Uganda, South Sudan, Equatorial Guinea, and the Central African Republic are among the African countries that have accepted third-country deportees.
The arrangements have triggered legal challenges across the continent. In June, rights lawyers sued Ghana at the Economic Community of West African States Community Court of Justice, accusing Accra of facilitating the onward removal of protected migrants to states where they faced abuse.
A US Senate Foreign Relations Committee minority report said Washington had sent more than $32 million to foreign governments in direct connection with third-country deportation deals by the end of January.
Liberia has said its participation is “entirely humanitarian,” pointing to its founding as a refuge for freed slaves from the US and elsewhere, as well as its history of sheltering people fleeing persecution and war.

Quarterly unemployment rate falls to 7.9 percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:16:13 UTC
21:16:13 KST

The figure was the lowest quarterly rate since 2005.
Türkiye’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declined by 0.3 percentage points from the previous quarter to 7.9 percent in the April-June period, the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) said on Aug. 19.
The figure was the lowest quarterly rate in the data series dating back to 2005.
The number of unemployed people aged 15 and over fell by 84,000 to 2.8 million. The unemployment rate was 6.7 percent among men and 10.3 percent among women.
Employment increased by 155,000 to 32.48 million, lifting the employment rate by 0.1 percentage points to 48.5 percent. The rate stood at 65.8 percent for men and 31.6 percent for women.
The labor force expanded by 71,000 to 35.28 million, while the participation rate edged down by 0.1 points to 52.7 percent.
Youth unemployment, covering those aged 15 to 24, fell by 1 percentage point to 13.9 percent. The rate was 11 percent among young men and 19.3 percent among young women.
The composite labor underutilization rate, which also includes time-related underemployment and the potential labor force, declined by 0.2 percentage points to 29.9 percent.

South Africa citrus exporters secure breakthrough in India

Unknown Publisher

21:07:33 KST

South Africa citrus exporters secure breakthrough in India
South African citrus exporters have received a boost in the Indian market after New Delhi amended its plant quarantine rules on Monday, approving additional cold-treatment options for fresh citrus imports from the African state.
The move, which follows almost a decade of negotiations, will give exporters more flexibility and could help improve the quality of fruit reaching the Indian market. Minister of Agriculture Willie Aucamp welcomed the development, saying it was good news for the industry and showed how technology was helping farmers overcome barriers and expand access to international markets.
He said it would help South African farmers push the boundaries and enable other countries to benefit from the country’s high-quality agricultural produce. “This is not only good news, but also indicates how advanced technology enable our farmers to push barriers to have other countries enjoy our high-quality produce,” Aucamp noted.
India is home to about 1.47 billion people and is one of the world’s largest and fastest-growing economies, making it a potentially important market for South African citrus.
CEO of the Citrus Growers’ Association of Southern Africa (CGA), Boitshoko Ntshabele, argued the focus should now shift to improving the commercial conditions for South African citrus exports to India. He said tariffs of about 25% to 30% continue to put South African citrus at a disadvantage compared with competitors from the Southern Hemisphere that have preferential trade arrangements with India.
“Special recognition is given to the Department of Agriculture and Citrus Research International for their continued technical engagement with Indian authorities that have made the new treatment options possible. This demonstrates the importance of sustained public-private partnership in improving technical conditions for accessing markets,” Ntshabele said.
“We look forward to working with the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition on the critical task of addressing these tariff barriers and improving the competitiveness of South African citrus in the Indian market going forward.”

'Something smells off': The Netanyahu backer behind two propaganda initiatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
12:06:10 UTC
21:06:10 KST

The name Avi Gross may not be the most immediately recognizable name among Benjamin Netanyahu's supporters. Yet he is the businessman behind at least two propaganda initiatives to disseminate the Likud's messages during election campaigns, a Haaretz investigation reveals.
Gross, who had been invited as a guest of honor to a Netanyahu speech before the U.S. Congress in 2024, is the man behind the content production company New Vision Production, located in Petah Tikva, central Israel. Establishing the studios with their advanced equipment had cost millions of shekels, sources confirmed to Haaretz. Gross himself declined to respond to Haaretz's inquiries.
Founded about a year ago, NVP operates along two separate but tangential tracks. One is to provide paid content services for the Likud campaign (which the party confirmed, stating that it was done legally). The second, as revealed by Haaretz, is the distribution of viral videos taken from podcasts that the company produces for Netanyahu-supporting media personalities. The Likud stated that the party has no connection to these podcasts, which leaves the question: who actually funds them?
There is also another track, perhaps only semi-official, where the company's premises serve as a kind of production house for ostensibly private videos that align with the campaign's messages (the party denies any connection). An analysis of these reveals that at least seven "content creators" filmed independent videos that, whether by chance or not, promoted the Likud campaign's messages and attacked Netanyahu's rivals and the media.
Some of the videos were produced even before the party contracted with the company. The list of creators includes, among others, Channel 14 reporter Tamir Schneid, panelist Noam Fathi, Likud spokesman Guy Levy, and Adi Shamai Hacohen – who was behind the "coming out" video "Mom, Dad, I'm a Bibist."
Since these are ostensibly private creators, "they are not subject to legal restrictions," a legal source involved in election law told Haaretz. But when everything is done in a single complex, the dots almost connect themselves: Welcome to the propaganda studios.
The current project is not the first time Gross has acted on Netanyahu's behalf in an election campaign. In 2021, he established Lychee Productions, which was behind "The Trial," a propaganda film distributed about a week before the November 2022 election that cast aspersions on the law enforcement system, "Case 4000" against Netanyahu, and the media. Over the years, Gross also published numerous posts on his social media accounts expressing support for Netanyahu and echoing his government's messages.
Gross, a 66-year-old resident of Mikhmoret, made his fortune in textiles, got into technology companies as a partner and founded the Panda mattresses company which he recently sold to Hollandia, in which he now holds 9 percent. He had been linked to the possible acquisition of the Maccabi Netanya soccer team but no deal ensued.
Gross is not officially connected to NVP. According to the Registrar of Companies, it was founded in July 2025 as "Neve Hadar Productions" by Neve Pinchas (who is defined as the company's CEO and, sources say, is responsible for content production). Until recently, the company had not been publicly credited with any product.
But this May, things moved quickly: its name was changed to NVP, it moved to Petah Tikva, it got a website and a month later, 90 percent of its shares were transferred to an American company whose owners' identity is unknown. The company, Great Production 2026 LLC, was incorporated in April in Delaware, which does not require shareholders to be divulged.
Although Gross does not appear in the company's documents at all, two sources well-versed in the details confirmed to Haaretz that he is the businessman behind the establishment of the media initiative in Petah Tikva.
Service vendors
Possibly, the word "initiative" does not adequately reflect the project's scale and scope of influence, especially how little the time it has been operating. In just five weeks, the company published dozens of short videos with pro-Netanyahu content, some of which garnered thousands of likes and tens of thousands of views. The sources of the videos are four new podcasts with at least 15 episodes.
The hosts include Netanyahu's brother Ido Netanyahu as well as personalities associated with media outlets such as Channel 14 and Galey Israel Radio, including Efi Mordechai – who brought us the "Ulpanometer," a venture to measure leftist presence on screen.
It doesn't end there. NVP also began providing services to Gadi Taub and his podcast group "Gatekeeper," featuring among others Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz. A new podcast called "The Nationalists," hosted by Alon Malik and Bat-El Benyamin, was recently added to the gallery of locally produced podcasts.
However, the studio recordings, all edited professionally, also include less regulated initiatives, where the only thing that seems orderly is the messages: a suspicious resemblance to the Likud campaign, and primarily – an attack on the mainstream media. For example, Channel 14 personality Noam Fathi filmed a propaganda video in the podcast studio against Channel 12 News (following a libel suit filed against him by the channel and Guy Peleg over his remarks regarding the Sde Teiman affair).
"Active Info" investigators, in collaboration with Haaretz, managed to verify by by means of geolocation and image comparison that additional propaganda videos were filmed in the Petah Tikva studio complex in recent months. For example, two government-supporting content creators, Yishai Gvirtzman and Dana Cohen, popularly dubbed "Dana Banana," filmed a video attacking the media from the complex's inner courtyard, which is only accessible after a security check and by invitation from someone working there.
Two other people who appear on the list of creators working there are spokesman Guy Levy and Tamir Schneid, Channel 14's "special affairs" reporter (going by the footage, it appears that at least one of the affairs is a clash over Case 4000). Both filmed in and outside the studios. At least in Levy's case, who echoed a message that Gadi Eisenkot – Netanyahu's main rival in the upcoming election – sought to end the war, the timing is key. He did so before July 27 but also after that date, and in the 90 days preceding the elections, election laws become critical.
The advent of NVP also changed the working method of Shamai Hacohen (from the "coming out" video). In June, even before the Likud began working with NVP, he switched his usual filming location from home to the studio in Petah Tikva. From there, for example, he launched an attack against Ronen Tzur, who called for Channel 14 to be shut down, or against media outlets that did not sufficiently sing Netanyahu's praises after the day of battle with Iran about two months ago.
Beyond the unofficial recordings, NVP is also responsible for official video content in the Likud campaign. So far, it has published about 20 videos in that context, mostly against Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot, incorporating two messages: "It's them or a broad national government" and "Eisenkot is not Yashar, he's left-wing." NVP is also responsible for the AI video showing Eisenkot running with outstretched arms toward a young man resembling his son who was killed in Gaza, but at the last moment he ignores him and embraces United Arab List chairman Mansour Abbas. The creator of this video is none other than Neve Pinchas, the company's founder, who still holds 10 percent of its shares.
"Something smells off," the legal source cognizant of election law told Haaretz. But asked if it goes beyond stink, he says it's a gray area, very much so. According to him, Israel's election laws are outdated and not suitable for 2026 and the social media era. Additionally, the fact that the videos aren't published by the party itself makes it hard to show connection between it and the distribution process.
Ultimately, he says, it will be a challenge to prove that the law had been broken. All will depend on the interpretation of the Central Elections Committee chairman, Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Solberg, and the evidence presented to him. "Part of the problem with current legislation is that the law doesn't apply to unofficial campaigns," he stresses. Thus they can bypass the law. "This is not the first time this has been done, but in the past, it was much more minor and subtle," he says.
On July 19, the members of the Likud Constitution, Law and Justice Committee received an invitation signed by Minister Haim Katz, to a special meeting to discuss the reserved slots the prime minister wanted on the party's Knesset slate. The location chosen for the gathering was NVP's offices in Petah Tikva. Ultimately the meeting was moved, but this does not mean the complex was erased from the Likud's map; on the contrary. Haaretz learned that in recent weeks, the studios have become a coveted destination for the prime minister himself.
In August alone, Netanyahu was documented there three times: once as a guest on Taub's podcast, a second time to film a video in which he announced a reserved slot for Oren Dobronsky on the Likud slate, and a third time for the strange story of the Army Radio program; last week, the military station published an episode of the podcast "King of Creating Life," featuring the prime minister, and for some reason, it was not filmed at the station's Jaffa base but in the Petah Tikva studios. The station explained that Netanyahu's office told them that the filming had to be moved due to security considerations. A security source told Haaretz that the Dignitary Protection Unit had not made any such demand.
Either way, according to several testimonies, Netanyahu's frequent visits to the studios cause difficulty and inconveniences for employees in the building. They receive no prior notice and before every visit, the Dignitary Protection Unit prevents employees from leaving their offices until filming is complete.
Getting credit
Another name arising in several contexts is attorney Ophir Falk, who became the prime minister's political adviser in 2023. The year before that, he partnered in the creation of Netanyahu's book "My Story," which was part of the election campaign that year and distributed in the week preceding it, and according to a source who spoke with Haaretz, he was paid for it from Sela Meir publishing house. The second – he was a partner in Lychee Productions (and held 30 percent of its shares until it was dissolved), and joined Gross in creating "The Trial." This film, which was promoted exclusively and primarily on the Walla website and social media – and also by Netanyahu himself – reached millions of views; all this just a few days before the elections.
Yinon Magal, host of "The Patriots" on Channel 14, was also involved in the film. His voice is not heard and his face does not appear on screen, but Haaretz learned that he received payment for his participation just six months before he testified for the prosecution in the Netanyahu trial. In fact, Magal, whose name appears in the credits at the end of the film, interviewed most of the participants.
Lychee, owned by Gross and Falk, invested significantly in promoting and distributing the film. It set up social media pages, disseminated video clips and of course marketed the 40-minute film itself. It was also distributed by Netanyahu and his son Yair, as well as among opinion leaders supporting the government, such as Taub, Galit Distel-Atbaryan, spokesman Guy Levy, and Magal himself, even though he did not state that he participated in the project. In early 2025, shortly before it was finally dissolved in March of that year, Lychee released a sequel, "The Trial 2," featuring some of the original film's participants. As often happens, the sequel did not reach the heights of the original film.
In addition to Avi Gross, NVP also declined to comment but last week it stated, "NVP is a leading production company. The company is engaged in producing independent content alongside providing professional production services to diverse clients. As a policy, the company does not discuss its clients' affairs or projects in the media. The company operates in compliance with all laws, and invites entities from across Israel's business, social, and public spectrum to enjoy its professional services."
Other subjects of the article did not provide responses either. Haaretz contacted the content creators filmed at NVP's complex and asked if they paid, received payment, or were connected to the company. Dana Cohen, Yishai Gvirtzman, Adi Shamai Hacohen, Natan Solomon, and Channel 14 reporter Tamir Schneid did not respond to the inquiry. Neither did Gadi Taub or Alon Malik, who were asked if the company pays them or if they pay the company for producing the podcasts.
Haaretz also contacted Yinon Magal, who provided an irrelevant response. Ophir Falk stated that "among the multitude of false claims, the most absurd is that the prime minister's book was written by me. Prime Minister Netanyahu wrote every single word in his book, and the proof of this is the original manuscript kept in his possession." However, a Haaretz inquiry reveals that Netanyahu wrote in his book that Falk typed the content during travels across the country.
The Likud stated in response that the party "legally hired NVP in accordance with all laws for election campaign productions," but the party did not respond to Haaretz's questions regarding the connection between Gross and Netanyahu.

"Are you serving in the IDF (Israeli army)? ... So I won’t discuss it. ... You guys are not even allowed to be in this country. And be grateful, because I’m not involving the police," Samir is heard saying in the viral footage.
Samir added that the Israelis enter Indonesia with a different passport.
In a follow-up video clarifying the exchange, the gym owner said the dispute began when one of the tourists acted rudely towards local staff members before confirming their nationality and military background.
"I said it was about Israelis and the IDF, not about religion. But they keep framing it as a religious issue," Samir said.
Samir reiterated that his facility maintains a strict policy against serving anyone who disrespects local employees or has served in the Israeli armed forces.
The incident comes against the backdrop of growing international backlash and boycotts targeting Israeli armed forces personnel amid Israel's ongoing genocide in the Palestinian enclave of Gaza.
Bali, Indonesia's primary tourism and cultural hub, hosts millions of international tourists and a large expatriate community each year, particularly in wellness destinations like Ubud.
Indonesia, the world’s most populous Muslim-majority nation, maintains no formal diplomatic or political relations with Israel, and Israeli passport holders face stringent entry restrictions.
Jakarta has consistently maintained a strong pro-Palestinian foreign policy, repeatedly demanding an immediate halt to Israeli military operations in Gaza.
Local law enforcement officials have stated they are examining the incident.
While Bali is renowned for its hospitality, local authorities and business operators have recently tightened scrutiny over tourist conduct and respect for local customs and workers.

Inside the slow ethnic cleansing of al-Mughayyir, a Palestinian village besieged by Israeli settlers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
11:58:34 UTC
20:58:34 KST

On a table set in the corner of the guest room, the cat belonging to Fadi Hamdallah al-Na’san, 17, climbs up and falls asleep among his belongings: his photographs, a collection of sports medals, and his school certificates. The small cat is still searching for her owner’s scent, still waiting for him to come home.
Fadi was declared a martyr on July 18, 2026, a week after being shot by Israeli forces while helping repel a settler attack on a home in his village of al-Mughayyir, east of Ramallah.
Since that day, the al-Na’san family’s home has declared open mourning for its child, hanging a large photo of him on the house. His parents cannot stop talking about the dream that he never got to fulfill.
“Despite his young age, the whole town loved Fadi and talks about him, remembering his character and how he got along with everyone,” Hamdallah al-Na’san, Fadi’s father, told Mondoweiss, his eyes wet, his voice barely holding steady. He shifted his weight on his crutches, wincing in pain from injuries inflicted by a settler attack decades ago that never fully healed.
The al-Na’san family’s home is not the only one in al-Mughayyir in mourning. Since October 2023, seven of the village’s sons have been killed and dozens arrested. Al-Mughayyir is considered one of the most prominent flashpoints of confrontation with settlers in the West Bank, given its strategic location between Ramallah and the Jordan Valley –surrounded on all sides by ten Israeli settlements and outposts.
Israeli military force and settler violence have become a daily feature of life in dozens of villages in the West Bank. According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, settler attacks and access restrictions have displaced Palestinians across 97 communities since January 2023, most of them Bedouin and herding communities. So-called Israeli “shepherding outposts” of settler-operated farms and grazing operations backed by the Israeli military have become one of the primary instruments for seizing Palestinian land, with settlers using violence and access restrictions to empty villages of their residents. In al-Mughayyir, that process is visible in real time.
Killed while protecting his neighbors
At 10 a.m. on July 12, 2026, calls rang out from the mosque loudspeakers in al-Mughayyir, urging villagers to come to the aid of the family of Abd al-Latif Abu Alia, whose home dozens of settlers were trying to storm. “Fadi went toward Abu Alia’s house, like everyone else,” Fadi’s father told Mondoweiss. “Before he reached the house, an Israeli army patrol was standing in the road. One of the soldiers got out and opened fire at Fadi, hitting him with a bullet in the leg, in the thigh area.”
Half an hour after the confrontations began – during which seven Palestinians were shot – news of Fadi’s injury reached his family. He was taken to the Palestine Medical Complex in Ramallah, suffering from a wound caused by an explosive bullet that had severed the arteries in his leg and caused severe bleeding.
“Fadi suffered several complications,” his father said. “He developed blood poisoning, and his kidneys and liver stopped functioning. Doctors decided to amputate his leg to keep the poisoning from spreading through the rest of his body. But his small body couldn’t withstand it all, and he was killed on the morning of July 18.”
Fadi, a boy full of energy and life, stood out as a talented player at the al-Mughayyir Football Academy and later qualified for the Palestinian youth national team, representing the central West Bank region. Mourning him, the Palestinian Football Federation described his murder as a severe loss for a sports community that has lost 1,013 players in Gaza and the West Bank since the war of extermination began on October 7, 2023, including 568 footballers killed.
“Fadi’s ambition was to play for the Palestinian national team and represent it on the world stage,” his father Hamdallah said. “But even so, he wasn’t consumed by football all the time — he was also a diligent student at school and was getting ready to move up to secondary school.”
This is not the first time the al-Na’san family has suffered attacks by the Israeli army and settlers. Twenty-seven years ago, a settler ran over Fadi’s father, Hamdallah, near Alon Road, which runs alongside al-Mughayyir. He still walks on crutches today and suffers severe pain in his back and legs.
“Our suffering didn’t end with losing Fadi,” Hamdallah said. “A week after he was killed, the Israeli army stormed our home and held us in one room, and detained our son Adib alone in another room, where they beat him repeatedly while we could hear him screaming. They then took him to a nearby military camp, where they continued torturing and beating him before releasing him several hours later.”
For days after his release, 19-year-old Adib’s body was aching from bruises and wounds resulting from beatings he endured, his morale broken.
Walls that don’t protect the people inside
Fadi is the second Palestinian from al-Mughayyir killed defending the Abu Alia family’s homes. On April 12, 2024, Jihad Afif Abu Alia, 25, was killed while helping the family repel a settler attack on their home, located in the al-Mughayyir plain on the village’s eastern edge. Since then, the family has surrounded its homes with a high fence and installed a gate at the entrance.
But during the settlers’ attack on July 12, 2026, Israeli soldiers tried to tear off the gate and remove the fence. Footage showed soldiers breaking the gate’s lock and damaging it in a way that prevents it from being closed again.
“Things have been getting worse for us day after day since 2023,” Abd al-Latif Abu Alia, 56, told Mondoweiss. “But recently the attacks have become daily, in the morning and the evening. Today, the settler wants to come in and graze his sheep in my home’s courtyard, and the army protects the settlers and gives them whatever they ask for — that’s why they want to remove the fence and leave our home exposed.”
The Abu Alia family is made up of 23 members across five households, including Abd al-Latif’s parents, both over 90 years old, and his brother, who has an intellectual disability. Their homes sit on five dunams (half a hectare) of land in the al-Mughayyir plain.
“All these attacks are meant to pressure us and force us out of our homes,” Abd al-Latif said. “But that’s impossible — we will not leave our home no matter what happens, and we have no alternative to it.”
When Mondoweiss visited, the family was gathered in front of their home, braced for any settler attack, as a settler grazed his sheep next to the house. Looking out at the settler, the family described all the injuries they have suffered in recent weeks: Abd al-Latif, two of his sons, and his brother Rasmi all have broken hands and arms from beatings by Israeli forces.
“On July 8, 15 Israeli soldiers stormed our home and beat us severely, which caused fractures in my hand,” Abd al-Latif said. “We were taken to the hospital, but refused to stay overnight, out of fear of leaving our women to face a settler attack alone. Every time we defend our homes against settler attacks, the army comes and punishes us by beating us, searching the house, and destroying its contents. All of us have also been arrested and detained many times.”
Amid the escalating settler attacks, Israeli Minister of National Security Itamar Ben Gvir visited one of the newer outposts built on al-Mughayyir’s land on July 13, 2026 – the day after the assault on the Abu Alia family, a nod of legitimacy to the settler attacks on al-Mughayyir, and and a show of support by the Israeli government to the attacks that settlers are carrying out against Palestinian villages.
Israel erases al-Mughayyir’s plains
The eastern plain of al-Mughayyir looks like a barren desert today. Before August 2025, it spanned 350 dunams (35 hectares) and was one of the main sources of income for al-Mughayyir’s residents. It has since suffered wide destruction by settlers and the Israeli army. The Abu Alia family alone lost 50 dunams (5 hectares) planted with olive trees.
Ghassan Jamal, of the al-Mughayyir Agricultural Cooperative Association, told Mondoweiss that Israel and its settlers have seized all the agricultural land and grazing areas in the eastern plain, the western plain, al-Qabun, al-Dalia, Marj al-Dhahab, and al-Rafid, making up some 42,000 dunams (4,200 hectares) in total and leaving al-Mughayyir’s residents with only 1,000 accessible dunams (100 hectares) in the area covered by the village’s master plan, classified as “Area B” under the Oslo Accords.
“In the eastern plain of al-Mughayyir, 12,000 olive trees have been uprooted,” Ghassan Jamal said. “They’ve also blocked villagers from reaching thousands of trees in the village’s other plains, behind Alon Road. In other areas, settlers pour toxic substances on the trees to kill them, and bring in sheep to graze on and destroy what remains.”
“Our grandparents planted al-Mughayyir’s trees, and we never let go of them — we inherited them generation after generation,” Jamal said. “All of al-Mughayyir’s land was cultivated and cared for by its people the whole time, which is why al-Mughayyir was like paradise, and its people depended on its trees as their main source of livelihood.”
Holding on to what remains of al-Mughayyir’s land, Jamal and 15 other farmers founded a cooperative association to help each other shoulder the burdens of the loss of their land. Their first project was planting golden thistle on six dunams (0.6 hectares) in the eastern plain. “As soon as it started to yield a crop, they stopped us from harvesting it,” he said, referring to Israeli authorities and settlers. “We planted 270 grapevines seven years ago, but within a few days, the settlers brought in sheep and destroyed them completely. They also targeted the association’s greenhouses, burning and destroying them.”
The destruction of al-Mughayyir’s livestock
Al-Mughayyir was not known only for its farmland, but also for its open grazing lands, which in the past allowed residents to own thousands of sheep. Jamal Abu Alia, a local farmer, said that al-Mughayyir once had more than 18,000 head of sheep, producing 2-3 tons of cheese every day.
Today, the Abu Hammam family is nearly the only one left in al-Mughayyir that still owns a flock of sheep. The size of their flock, however, has halved in recent years, falling to only 130 heads, as a result of the family being barred from reaching grazing land.
Since October 2023, the Hammam family has been forced, due to threats from settlers, to move from their home in al-Mughayyir village to their two dunams of land in the al-Khalayel area. But in December 2025, settlers launched a violent attack on the family, beating them and driving them off the land, which they are unable to reach today.
“Today there’s no grazing land for the sheep, which stay in the pen all the time, multiplying the cost for us significantly,” Fatima Abu Naim told Mondoweiss. “We’re able to stay in our home in the middle of al-Mughayyir, but we’re afraid that settlers will reach our land here too and take it, the way they took our land in al-Khalayel and the eastern plain. But we’re trying to bear the hardship of life and stay here, so we can keep settlers from reaching this place.”
Fatima, a mother of five, voices the fears of every family in al-Mughayyir. “Every day that passes in al-Mughayyir is worse than the one before it. We live in constant fear, anxiety, and readiness for any attack,” Fatima said.
“I used to think about my children’s future and work so I could help them get an education and achieve their dreams. But today I’m consumed by fear for them, for their lives, and for their existence.”

Muratağa and Sandallar Cemetery of Martyrs in Northern Cyprus (AA photo)
A group of Greek Cypriot politicians has called for a reckoning with the past and mutual apologies over attacks and massacres targeting Turkish Cypriots, noting that that those responsible have largely gone unpunished.
Former Greek Cypriot Foreign Minister Erato Kozakou-Marcoullis this week reposted on social media a 2016 post featuring photographs from a mass grave and issued remarks on the Turkish Cypriots massacred by Greek Cypriot armed groups in the villages of Aloda (Atlılar), Maratha (Muratağa), Sandallaris (Sandallar) and Tochni (Taşkent) on Aug. 14, 1974.
Marcoullis said that no Greek Cypriot had been punished for the killings of Turkish Cypriots, calling for the truth to be acknowledged and for both communities to apologize to one another.
“Let us acknowledge the truth and apologize to each other,” she said.
Warning that the far right continues to pose a threat on the island, Marcoullis wrote: “Unpunished crimes, unspoken truths, wounds that have not healed, pain that has not subsided.”
She stressed the need to acknowledge the facts, saying that unless the truth is confronted, crimes remain buried in silence and the suffering of both communities is acknowledged, “the divide will widen, peace will not be built, and the vision of a common homeland will forever elude us.”
Greek Cypriot lawmaker Giorgos Koukoumas also said in a written statement that the attacks against Turkish Cypriots represented one of the lesser-known chapters of Greek Cyprus’ history and could no longer be ignored by the Greek Cypriot community.
Koukoumas described the killing of 126 Turkish Cypriot women, children and elderly people by Greek Cypriot armed groups in the Famagusta area villages in August 1974, as well as the killing of a large number of Turkish Cypriot men in Tochni, as “one of the darkest pages in history.”
He said the attacks were carried out by Greek Cypriot far-right elements and stressed that most of those responsible had never been brought to justice.
“No person with a basic sense of human dignity, regardless of their political views or position on the Cyprus issue, can ignore questions such as how Turkish Cypriot children were found collectively in wells and how their remains are still being unearthed today,” Koukoumas said.
The politicians’ social media posts received support from parts of the Greek Cypriot public as well as from some politicians in the Greek Cypriot community.
Türkiye launched its 1974 Peace Operation following a coup backed by the military junta in Greece that sought to unite Cyprus with Greece. Ankara said the operation was carried out to restore constitutional order and protect the Turkish Cypriot community after years of intercommunal violence.
Following the division of the island, the Turkish Cypriot administration in the north has been recognized solely by Türkiye.

Ukrainian anti-corruption agencies said Wednesday they are investigating senior officials in President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office, a day after the country's recently fired defense minister called for national elections despite the war with Russia.
The political drama was an unwelcome distraction for Zelenskyy as Ukraine's war with its bigger neighbor stretches into its fifth year.

The revelation brought another test of Zelenskyy's political resilience as he remains dogged by high-level graft investigations.

Zelenskyy, seeking to reconcile tensions between the defense ministry's young and tech-savvy innovators and Ukraine's seasoned, Soviet-trained battlefield leaders, risked angering both sides by reshuffling his wartime leadership.

He said Ukraine is facing a systemic crisis in how it is governed, arguing that the current system is oriented toward protecting itself and resisting change.
He also condemned corruption among officials without naming anyone, saying it had weakened Ukraine's ability to fight the war.
Zelenskyy's office did not immediately comment on Fedorov's address. It was not immediately clear whether Fedorov's appeal for a ballot would resonate with Ukrainians.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, who has balked at negotiating a peace deal directly with Zelenskyy, says the Ukrainian president is an illegitimate leader because his term expired in 2024.
Fedorov published his speech hours after Ukraine's Parliament received Zelenskyy's formal nomination of Yevhenii Khmara as the new defense minister, a move that effectively closes the door to Fedorov's return to the post, which he has sought, any time soon.
Lawmakers were due to debate the president's candidate Wednesday.
The political disarray comes after recent successes in the war for Ukraine. Using its innovative drone technology, it has repeatedly hit Russian oil facilities, causing fuel shortages.
It has also shocked the Russian public by striking warehouses of Wildberries, Russia's biggest online retailer, and stalled front-line advances by Russia's bigger army.
But Zelenskyy has been unable to get traction in U.S.-led peace efforts and Ukraine is at the mercy of Russia's ballistic missiles because more U.S.-made Patriot interceptors aren't available due to low international stockpiles.

The city of Ufa is located roughly 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) east of the border with Ukraine. There are three oil refineries in Ufa, and all three have been attacked before.
Russian air defenses overnight intercepted 453 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions, as well as occupied Crimea and the Black Sea, the Defense Ministry in Moscow said Wednesday.
The Defense Ministry said Russian forces Tuesday evening hit a bulk carrier in the Black Sea, southeast of Odesa, that was carrying military equipment.
On Wednesday, the Russian military struck what it said were fuel and lubricant storage tanks for the Ukrainian armed forces in the southern port of Chornomorsk.
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a Russian drone attacked a minibus in the southern Kherson region on Wednesday morning, killing four people, said Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson regional military administration.
Four women were also wounded in the strike and were hospitalized, he said.
Also, a Russian drone struck a civilian car in Kherson city, the region's capital, on Wednesday, killing a woman, said Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson regional military administration.
Amid the fighting, Russia and Ukraine each sent home 103 prisoners of war Wednesday, according to the Russian Defense Ministry.

Tiny quantum engines reveal useful energy hiding in “waste heat”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
11:49:52 UTC
20:49:52 KST

Tiny quantum engines reveal useful energy hiding in “waste heat”
- Date:
- August 19, 2026
- Source:
- University of Basel
- Summary:
- A tiny machine made from just an atom and particles of light may sound impossibly simple, but it raises a surprisingly difficult question: what counts as heat, and what energy can still do useful work? University of Basel researchers have developed a theoretical framework that brings quantum physics and thermodynamics into better agreement for these microscopic “light engines.”
- Share:
What counts as heat, and what qualifies as useful work when a machine is made from only an atom and particles of light? In emerging quantum technologies, questions like this bring together two branches of physics that were developed for very different purposes. Researchers at the University of Basel in Switzerland have now introduced a theoretical framework designed to make thermodynamics and quantum physics work consistently in the same setting.
Thermodynamics emerged in the 19th century largely to explain how large machines such as steam engines convert and transfer energy. Quantum physics, developed in the early 20th century, instead focuses on atoms and subatomic particles. Today, however, the two fields increasingly overlap. Tiny systems built from atoms and light particles (photons) can take in energy, transform it, and release it, allowing them to function as microscopic quantum machines.
A major challenge is finding a description that remains valid both when the entire system is treated quantum mechanically and in the semi-classical limit. The latter is the limiting case in which one part of the system is treated quantum mechanically, while classical physics is sufficient for the other part. Researchers in the group of Professor Patrick Potts at the University of Basel have now presented such an approach in Physical Review Letters.
A Tiny Quantum Light Engine
"Our calculations regard the concrete physical model of an atom that is placed in a cavity between two mirrors, where it can absorb and emit light particles," says postdoc Marcelo Janovitch. In this setup, a laser continuously supplies additional photons to the cavity, while some light escapes through the partially reflecting mirrors.
"This is a textbook example of a so-called driven-dissipative system that continuously receives energy and simultaneously loses it to the environment," says the researcher. The model gives physicists a way to investigate fundamental questions involving open quantum systems. In this case, the atom behaves much like a miniature heat engine, or more specifically, a "light engine."
Potts and his collaborators had previously shown that photons leaving the cavity should not automatically be treated as "waste heat" in a thermodynamic description. Some of the energy carried by that escaping light can still be used to perform useful work on another quantum system.
Their latest study examined what happens to this distinction between heat and useful energy when the system approaches the semi-classical limit.
Separating Useful Energy From Heat
In the semi-classical limit, the atom inside the cavity continues to be treated as a quantum system with discrete energy levels. The light, however, is treated as a classical electromagnetic wave, meaning its quantum effects can be ignored.
"Treating the light classically makes it much easier to define which part of the energy can be used to perform work and which part is disordered heat," says Janovitch. For the theory to be consistent, this classical limiting behavior should emerge naturally from the full quantum thermodynamic description.
Janovitch and his colleagues have now demonstrated mathematically that this is possible with their approach. When part of the emitted light is classified as useful work, the theory moves smoothly into the semi-classical limit.
The conventional approach produces a different result. If all energy leaving the cavity is counted as heat, the theory does not make the same consistent transition.
Quantum Fluctuations Become a Resource
The researchers also found that their calculations correctly describe how quantum effects can reduce fluctuations in the emitted light particles.
These reduced fluctuations could be especially valuable for quantum technologies. Heat often creates disturbances that make quantum systems harder to control, but under the right conditions, it could instead become a useful resource.
For example, the effect could help produce particular states of light that are useful for especially precise measurements in quantum metrology. The findings show how a better understanding of the boundary between heat and useful work could help researchers take advantage of energy that might otherwise appear to be lost.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Basel. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Marcelo Janovitch, Sander Stammbach, Matteo Brunelli, Patrick P. Potts. Bridging Quantum and Semiclassical Thermodynamics in Cavity QED. Physical Review Letters, 2026; 137 (7) DOI: 10.1103/y6h7-sx93

The letter was signed by the Assembly of Turkish American Associations, the Turkish American Coalition, the Federation of Turkish American Associations, the Turkish American National Steering Committee, MUSIAD USA, the Turkish American Chamber of Commerce of the South and ASKON USA.
The groups noted that U.S.-Türkiye relations date to 1831 and that Ankara has been a formal treaty ally since joining NATO in 1952, “anchoring the Alliance’s southeastern border and controlling the Bosporus and Dardanelles.”
The letter pointed to Turkish bases, including Incirlik, as “indispensable to defeating ISIL” and noted that Turkish forces “fought and died alongside American troops” during the Korean War.
The organizations argued that approving the sale of F-35 jets “keeps Ankara anchored to U.S. and NATO-aligned suppliers rather than alternatives” as Europe rearms and Türkiye’s defense industry grows.
The letter also cited Türkiye’s role as a “constructive regional actor, including its mediation role in the Russia-Ukraine war, its pursuit of peace with the PKK, its involvement in stability efforts in Syria and its rapprochement with Armenia.
The letter was delivered to over 50 members of Congress in July.

In Ukraine, forcible military recruitment efforts escalate into violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
11:47:44 UTC
20:47:44 KST

In Ukraine, forcible military recruitment efforts escalate into violence
‘Busification’, the term describing being captured on the street, is engulfed by abuse and corruption.
Anton was walking home with a friend in Kyiv when he was suddenly seized and forced into the back seat of a police car, with an officer on each side, heading towards a future that would likely see him in the trenches.
The 52-year-old, who requested to withhold his surname to protect his identity, has supported Ukraine’s fight against Russia, but did not want to be sent to the front line. The grinding attrition of war seemed like a death sentence given his health issues. He is HIV-positive and has arthritis and poor eyesight – conditions that he believed made him medically unfit to serve.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Russian missile attacks kill at least nine in Ukraine’s Kyiv
- list 2 of 4Moscow restaurant bombing kills three
- list 3 of 4Russian and Ukrainian strikes kill 14 on both sides
- list 4 of 4Ukraine strikes Russia’s biggest retailer again
But since mobilisation laws took effect in May 2024, Ukraine’s recruitment officers have been ambushing men on the street.
In late January, when he was allegedly captured, he had been avoiding venturing out of his apartment block – fearful of both Ukraine’s controversial conscription drive and Russian drone attacks on his neighbourhood.
But on one of the few times he did leave his home, the police jumped out of a car that was parked in a residential garage and chased him, he said.
He was then caught and driven to a militarised section of a state clinic in Kyiv, where his phone was confiscated.
“They told me to mute my phone and hand it over,” he said. “I started to protest. The guard said, ‘Don’t push me to use physical methods on you. Give it to me now.’ So I did.”
After undergoing medical tests, he was transferred to a military recruitment centre on the outskirts of the city, where he would spend two days in a room with barred windows, a bucket of cold pasta, and no way to contact the outside world.
What happened to Anton has a term in Ukraine – “busification” – men stopped on city streets, checked for exemption cards, and placed directly onto buses bound for mobilisation centres.
According to observers, as Ukraine’s conscription crisis grows, it is increasingly common.
On the streets, resistance against the recruitment officers has also turned physical, and on occasion, deadly.
Within the space of three days in February, a draft officer was shot dead at a petrol station in Poltava oblast, an explosion inside a draft office in Rivne killed one person and wounded six, and another blast wounded one at an enlistment office in Pavlohrad. Ukraine’s Security Service later said Russia had recruited the perpetrator of the Rivne bombing.
At the military recruitment centre, Anton watched on as young men arrived, freshly caught from the streets with stories to tell.
One man told him he had been seized hours earlier, as he prepared to drive his wife to hospital to give birth to their first child.
“There was a strong sense of solidarity,” he told Al Jazeera. “They shared their life stories and tried to offer advice and share their opinions, as well as their experiences of dealing with the guards.”
As recruitment officers began parcelling the men out to military units, Anton discovered that his HIV status had been withheld from the commanders they were being offered to – information that, once revealed, saw him deemed too unwell to serve.
He was eventually released, but said it cost him $5,000 in lawyers’ fees to walk free on a conditional summons, and a further $30,000 paid to fixers who promised to secure his documents and then vanished.
He is now confined to his home, afraid to step outside.
At the time of publishing, the Command of the Territorial Defence Forces had not responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
In the months following Russia’s full-scale invasion, initial battlefield successes and a wave of patriotism led to hundreds of thousands volunteering to serve, but after a failed counteroffensive in 2023, recruitment became difficult, and tactics hardened.
Two laws signed in April 2024 lowered the draft age from 27 to 25, quintupled fines for evasion, and dropped a promised provision that would have allowed soldiers to demobilise after 36 months of service, leaving those already fighting with no fixed end to their duty.
Men have reportedly been taken from a range of sites.
In October 2024, footage outside a concert at Kyiv’s Palace of Sports showed officers dragging a man across the pavement as onlookers chanted “Shame!”
In the western city of Uzhhorod, a man was rounded up as he left Sunday mass despite carrying papers proving he was the sole carer for his disabled mother.
Corruption in the recruitment process has been alleged. In some cases, men have obtained exemptions through paid-for medical diagnoses.
In October 2024, Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Andriy Kostin resigned after journalists reported that dozens of prosecutors in the western Khmelnytskyi region held disability status to avoid the draft.
The scandal proved to be the tip of the iceberg: Ukraine’s security service announced it had cancelled 4,106 fake disability certificates issued through corrupt medical examination commissions that year, charging 64 commission officials in the process.
Then, in January 2025, the chief psychiatrist of Ukraine’s armed forces – a senior member of the central military medical commission that decides whether conscripts are fit to serve – was arrested for illegal enrichment, having accumulated a house, apartments in Kyiv and Odesa, land, and four luxury cars worth more than $1m since the invasion began.
Investigators searching his home found $152,000 and 34,000 euros in cash.
‘Systematic and large-scale’
The alleged abuses have been documented internationally.
In a memorandum published on July 8, 2025, the Council of Europe’s commissioner for human rights raised alarm over mobilisation practices, including beatings, harsh detentions, denial of access to lawyers, and the conscription of men with disabilities, citing Ukraine’s parliamentary human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, who had described the violations as “systematic and large-scale”.
This has affected public opinion.
According to a July 2025 survey by Ukraine’s Rating Group, only 24 percent of Ukrainians said they trusted enlistment officers.
Telegram groups began tracking recruiters in real time – a movement so popular that Google’s Threat Analysis Group identified a suspected Russian intelligence operation piggybacking on it in October 2024, creating a fake app that purported to map recruiters’ locations while secretly installing malware.
Attacks on recruitment officers
More than 600 attacks on enlistment officers have been recorded since the start of the war, with assaults nearly tripling in 2025.
The first four months of 2026 alone saw 117 – more than 20 times the five recorded in the war’s entire first year.
Anger has boiled over.
On July 8, 2026, a crowd in Lviv’s Sykhiv district blocked, damaged and overturned a recruitment service vehicle during the detention of a man wanted for draft evasion, prompting pre-trial investigations by the national police and the Security Service of Ukraine.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has argued that the only beneficiary of such scenes is Russia.
Yet the condemnations have also been tempered with concessions by institutions like the Defence Ministry, which conceded that mobilisation methods need improvement.
Oleksandr Syrskii, who was sacked as the country’s commander-in-chief last month along with the defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, also acknowledged the army was working to correct mistakes and prevent rights violations at enlistment offices.

Syria says it can stop buying wheat abroad, but analysts say the reality is more complicated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
11:46:09 UTC
20:46:09 KST

Syria says the sharp increase in wheat production during the 2026 season could allow it to significantly reduce its reliance on imports and, at least as far as the Syrian Grain Establishment’s needs are concerned, potentially eliminate them altogether this season.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Such a shift could ease pressure on the country’s limited foreign currency reserves and reduce one aspect of Syria’s direct economic dependence on Russia, a major supplier of wheat used in the country’s bread system for years.
Purchases of domestically grown wheat by the Syrian Grain Establishment have reached about 2.7 million tons, exceeding the agency's stated annual requirement of roughly 2.55 million tons. That has prompted officials to say the establishment no longer needs to sign new import contracts for the current season.
But the announcement that imports are no longer needed raised new questions about what the claim of self-sufficiency actually means. On August 11, a new shipment of wheat arrived at the Port of Tartus through Pier 4. The identity of the importer and the original source of the wheat were not immediately clear, nor was it known whether the shipment was linked to a contract signed before the Grain Establishment announced that it had covered its requirements, or whether it was intended for needs outside the establishment’s purchases.
The shipment does not necessarily contradict the establishment’s statements. It could be tied to an earlier contract, intended for strategic reserves, or consist of varieties and quantities not covered by domestic procurement. But its arrival highlights the need to distinguish between the Grain Establishment covering its own requirements and Syria as a whole ending wheat imports.
The latest harvest follows a difficult 2025 agricultural season
The improvement in this year’s harvest follows an exceptionally difficult agricultural season in 2025, when drought caused wheat production to fall sharply and increased Syria’s need for imports. According to Agriculture Ministry data, wheat production that season stood at around 934,000 tons.
For 2026, however, the ministry estimates a final production figure of more than 3 million tons, driven by improved rainfall and the return of large areas to cultivation, particularly in regions that have traditionally served as major centers of grain production.
But the official figures raise a fundamental question: Does the Syrian Grain Establishment’s ability to meet its needs mean that Syria has actually regained wheat self-sufficiency?
Economist Yafa Nawaf told The Media Line that the Grain Establishment’s purchases reaching roughly 2.7 million tons are not, by themselves, enough to conclude that the country has restored self-sufficiency, because that figure represents what the agency purchased from farmers rather than total national production or the country’s overall consumption.
The Grain Establishment says its annual requirement is about 2.55 million tons. On that basis, Nawaf said, the agency can meet its own needs without importing wheat this season.
The picture becomes more complicated, however, when those figures are compared with earlier estimates placing Syria’s total annual wheat consumption at around 4 million tons.
Nawaf said the difference—about 1.45 million tons between the Grain Establishment’s stated requirement and the estimated national consumption—suggests that the two figures measure different things.
“The first figure most likely refers to the quantities the government establishment needs to supply flour and bread through its own system, while the second includes the country’s overall consumption and other uses of wheat,” she said. “Therefore, the claim that imports are no longer needed may be accurate in terms of the Grain Establishment’s requirements for the 2026 season, but it is not sufficient on its own to prove that Syria has achieved full national self-sufficiency.”
According to Nawaf, establishing self-sufficiency at the national level would require a clear wheat balance showing total production, existing stocks, consumption, quantities reserved for seed, losses, and volumes traded outside the government procurement system.
That distinction is important because the Grain Establishment purchasing more than its own annual requirement does not necessarily mean that the country’s total domestic wheat supply covers every form of consumption.
The surge should be interpreted cautiously, Nawaf says
The 2026 season nevertheless represents a dramatic change from the previous year. If production indeed surpasses 3 million tons after reaching only around 934,000 tons in 2025, wheat output has more than tripled in a single year.
Nawaf said the surge should be interpreted cautiously because a substantial part of it resulted from improved rainfall and the return of large areas to cultivation, rather than solely from permanent structural improvements in Syria’s agricultural sector.
Farmers’ ability to repeat current production levels will also depend on whether wheat remains economically viable.
According to the Ministry of Economy and Industry, figures cited for the current season show that the wheat purchase price was set at about 46,000 new Syrian pounds per ton, with an additional bonus of 9,000 pounds, bringing the total return to roughly 55,000 pounds per ton.
Nawaf noted, however, that a higher nominal purchasing price does not necessarily guarantee that wheat farming will remain profitable next season. Final production costs depend on the prices of seed, fertilizer, fuel, irrigation, harvesting, and transportation.
That becomes particularly relevant in years with less rainfall, when farmers must rely more heavily on irrigation and absorb the additional costs.
Nawaf said sustainably eliminating the need for wheat imports depends on more than one successful season. It requires continued support for producers, access to fertilizer, seed, and fuel at affordable prices, and investment in irrigation networks, dams, and storage capacity.
Without those measures, she said, self-sufficiency could remain dependent on rainfall and fluctuate sharply from one agricultural season to the next.
The importance of this year’s wheat season extends beyond food security to the finances of a country with limited access to foreign currency.
Syrian political activist Mufida Ankair, who lives in Germany and follows changes in Russia’s presence in Syria, told The Media Line that Damascus’ ability to reduce or halt wheat imports could ease significant pressure on its foreign currency reserves.
The Food and Agriculture Organization had estimated that Syria would need to import around 3 million tons of wheat during the 2025-2026 season after drought sharply reduced domestic production.
At international prices of approximately $250 to $300 per ton, importing 3 million tons could cost between $750 million and $900 million, before shipping, insurance, and financing expenses.
Ankair said replacing a large share of those imports with domestic production could save Syria hundreds of millions of dollars while also reducing its exposure to fluctuations in international commodity prices and disruptions in global supply chains.
Reduced import requirements also carry broader implications for Damascus’ relationship with Moscow. During the war and its aftermath, Russia became a major wheat supplier to Syria, and grain shipments developed into part of a broader network of economic and political ties between the two countries.
But Ankair cautioned against interpreting reduced reliance on Russian wheat as the beginning of an economic separation between Syria and Russia. Russia remains an important supplier to Syria in other sectors, particularly energy, she said, while commercial, military, and logistical ties between the two countries extend far beyond grain.
“Reduced dependence on Russian wheat lessens one form of Syria’s direct reliance on Russia, but it does not mean that the economic relationship between the two countries has ended or fundamentally changed,” she said.

The announcement came after Turkish Minister of National Defense Yaşar Güler and his Syrian counterpart, Murhaf Abu Qasra, signed a memorandum of understanding. The document provides for cooperation in providing military support to Syria.
Earlier, in February 2025, Syria’s new authorities proposed that Turkey establish air bases in the country to replace Russia.
In addition, Turkey would be allowed to use Syrian airspace for military purposes and would undertake to provide assistance in the event of external threats.
